source.title: Grammar-Constrained Decoding Can Jailbreak LLMs into Generating Malicious Code
source.authors: Yi-Tong Zhang; Shiteng Lu; Jia Li

page_placements.theme: Code, encodings and task reformulations bypass safeguards

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether a decoding intervention can bypass safety on harmful code requests, using grammar-constrained decoding rather than fine-tuning, prefilling, suffixes, or token-position measurements.
record.gate_note: The paper reports CodeSpear attack outcomes under grammar-constrained decoding and compares them with Vanilla. It also reports a tightened-grammar variant and CodeShield defense results. No results measure fine-tuning on small harmful or benign datasets, per-token KL, prefilling, suffixes, decoding changes other than GCD, parameter localization, or first-token depth.
record.test_reason: The study shows that grammar-constrained decoding (GCD) on malicious code requests raises harmful-code rates. V4 names prefilling a compliant start, suffixes or decoding changes that defeat refusal. GCD does not prefill or alter an opening. It removes natural-language refusals from the output space, so it is a different mechanism. The study never ties its results to opening tokens or shallow alignment. Its stated explanation is that alignment is grounded in the natural-language modality. It also reports no per-token or first-token measurements. It cites the Qi et al. shallow-alignment paper only in passing. I judge it a related but different construct (an output-space constraint on code), so no version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that benign GCD can jailbreak LLMs into malicious code because alignment is grounded in natural-language refusals. They also conclude that CodeShield (honeypot-code DPO) restores safety while preserving utility. The record omits the adaptive-attack result (Table VI, CodeShield robust).
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates grammar-constrained decoding as a jailbreak, not harmful or benign fine-tuning, token-position KL, or prefix bypass. It also trains a separate defense using DPO preferences involving honeypot code.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack results vary by model and benchmark. GPT-5 and GPT-5-mini have lower ASR than other API models; tightening the grammar to disallow pass increases ASR and MR. The paper also reports CodeSpear under Python, C++, and Java grammars, but the associated figure gives no extractable numeric values in the text.

fits_no_version.finding: Applying an off-the-shelf benign Python grammar via GCD raises ASR and MR on malicious code requests across 10 models. The average gain is +26.9 ASR points for local models and +45.4 for API models. GPT-5 models rise less. LLaMA3-8B MalwareBench MR drops from 33.96% to 26.98%. A tightened grammar that disallows pass raises rates further.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Grammar-constrained decoding to code-only output can bypass refusal in malicious code generation.

fits_no_version.finding: DPO on honeypot code restores safety under GCD: average ASR falls from 83.11% to 5.57% on Qwen2.5-Coder-7B. Standard refusal DPO (Safe-DPO) stays at 77.39%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Modality-specific safety training can defend against GCD-based bypass.

record.problems: Main ASR and MR tables do not report error bars or confidence intervals, although experiments are repeated three times and averages are reported. Safety judgments use an LLM judge; manual evaluation of 100 sampled responses agrees at 87% for ASR and 85% for MR. The paper notes that GCD implementations and evaluated malicious-request benchmarks do not cover every setting.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 3 reports average ASR for Python, C++, and Java grammar conditions without textual numeric values; it states that CodeSpear raises ASR above 70% on Qwen2.5-Coder-7B under each grammar, but does not provide per-grammar values. Figure 4 reports CodeShield results across honeypot sample counts K without textual numeric values. Adaptive-attack Table VI reports CodeShield outcomes under tightened grammars; omitted because the kept CodeShield rows already capture the main defense result and the adaptive table adds no distinct grammar-jailbreak claim beyond its aggregate presentation.

untested.parts: Fine-tuning on harmful examples; not tested.
Prefilling, suffixes and non-GCD decoding changes; not tested.
Cause of shallowness in data or objective; not tested.
Deepening safety beyond early tokens; CodeShield is a code-modality DPO defense, not a test of this.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V4 'tested' status and its labels should be dropped. The reader's verdicts, including 'challenges' for CodeShield, are not supported. A defense working against the study's own attack says nothing about V4. Results are single-judge LLM evaluations with no confidence intervals.

versions.untested_parts: Fine-tuning safety-trained models on harmful examples and measuring compliance.
Fine-tuning on ordinary or carefully selected benign data and measuring harmful compliance.
Per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models on harmful prompts.
Prefilled compliant openings, adversarial suffixes, and decoding changes other than grammar-constrained decoding.
Whether safety behavior is localized in a small set of weights or ranks.
Whether training data or objective causes first-token shallowness.
Training safety to extend beyond early response tokens and measuring whether that depth holds up.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-Coder-7B
rows.operation_detail: CodeSpear applies grammar-constrained decoding with an off-the-shelf Python grammar
rows.check: These rows measure GCD-induced malicious code generation, which is not the V4 mechanism of prefilling, suffixes or decoding changes that skip the refusal opening. Move the finding to fits_no_version. If a reviewer accepts GCD as a V4 decoding change, the per-row states are mostly right. The exceptions are r20 (reversed) and r32, r34, r36, r40, which have only 1/2 numbers found.

relation.reason: The study experimentally compares harmful-code generation with and without grammar-constrained decoding. Table IV reports unmodified Qwen2.5-Coder-7B average ASR increasing from 28.36% without CodeSpear to 83.11% with CodeSpear, directly bearing on V4.

tranche.reason: CodeSpear tests V4 through a different decoding intervention: grammar constraints exclude natural-language refusals and increase harmful compliance. V4 explicitly includes decoding changes; prefilling an opening is not required.

source_check.notes: The listed defense comparisons do not establish V7 because they do not measure safety spreading beyond the first tokens. Study-wide attack results support V4 in the tested settings; no verdicts were listed in the pack.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Standard CodeSpear grammar-constrained decoding across the tested local and API models and benchmarks
reader_labels.reason: CodeSpear raises ASR in nearly all tested model-benchmark cases and raises MR in nearly all cases; see r01-r19 and r21-r40.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: GPT-5 and GPT-5-mini, and cases where CodeSpear only modestly raises outcomes or MR falls
reader_labels.reason: The paper reports lower ASR for GPT-5 and GPT-5-mini than other API models, several small increases, and one lower MR result; see r05-r10, r15-r16, r18-r24, r31-r34, and r20.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Tightened grammar disallowing pass on GPT-5 and GPT-5-mini
reader_labels.reason: Removing a common safe code pattern further increases both ASR and MR for both models on both benchmarks; see r41-r48.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.reason: CodeShield reduces average ASR and MR under the attack substantially, unlike the bypass prediction; see r49-r50.
